title: Πατρόκλου τελευτή
about: Noon passes and the Achaeans begin to prevail; Patroclus kills twenty-seven men in three rushes, but at the fourth Apollo, hidden in mist, strikes him on the back, knocks off his helmet, shatters his spear and looses his breastplate. Stunned, he is wounded from behind by the Dardanian Euphorbus, and Hector comes up and drives a spear through his flank; the poet likens it to a lion overpowering a boar over a spring. Hector taunts the dying man, who answers that the gods and Euphorbus killed him, that Hector is only the third, and that Hector's own death is near. Patroclus dies, and Hector, pulling out his spear, goes after Automedon, whom the deathless horses of Peleus carry out of reach.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν Ἠέλιος μέσον οὐρανὸν ἀμφιβεβήκει,
τόφρα μάλ’ ἀμφοτέρων βέλε’ ἥπτετο, πῖπτε δὲ λαός·
sentences.l:
So long as the Sun had bestridden the middle of heaven,
for that time the missiles of both sides took hold, and the people fell;
sentences.i: As long as the Sun stood in the middle of heaven, for that time the missiles of both sides struck home, and the army fell;
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα are correlatives, ‘as long as … for so long’. Ἠέλιος is the epic form of Ἥλιος ‘the Sun’, and ἀμφιβεβήκει, the pluperfect of ἀμφιβαίνω ‘bestride’, says that he has taken his stand astride the middle of heaven and is still there, i.e. noon. Line 778 is a line already met: ἥπτετο is the imperfect middle of ἅπτω ‘take hold’, said of missiles that find their mark, and βέλε’ is βέλεα with its last vowel elided. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ Ἠέλιος μετενίσετο βουλυτὸν δέ,
καὶ τότε δή ῥ’ ὑπὲρ αἶσαν Ἀχαιοὶ φέρτεροι ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
And when the Sun turned toward the ox-unyoking time,
then indeed beyond due measure the Achaeans were stronger.
sentences.i: But when the Sun turned toward the time for unyoking oxen, then the Achaeans proved stronger beyond what was due.
sentences.n: ἦμος ‘when’ is the epic conjunction, and βουλυτὸν δέ is βουλυτόνδε, ‘toward the time for unyoking oxen’, that is evening, with the ending -δε of motion toward. μετενίσετο is the imperfect of a verb meaning ‘go over to, pass on to’ (μετανίσσομαι). ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ‘beyond due measure’ is the opposite of κατ’ αἶσαν ‘in due measure’; αἶσα is a person’s allotted portion. φέρτεροι is the comparative ‘stronger’, ‘mightier’ in force, agreeing with Ἀχαιοί.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μὲν Κεβριόνην βελέων ἥρωα ἔρυσσαν
Τρώων ἐξ ἐνοπῆς, καὶ ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἕλοντο,
Πάτροκλος δὲ Τρωσὶ κακὰ φρονέων ἐνόρουσε.
sentences.l:
Out of the missiles Cebriones the hero they drew,
out of the Trojans’ shouting, and from his shoulders the armour they took,
and Patroclus, with evil in his mind for the Trojans, rushed on.
sentences.i: The Achaeans drew the hero Cebriones out of the missiles, out of the shouting of the Trojans, and took the armour from his shoulders, but Patroclus rushed on the Trojans with evil in his mind.
sentences.n: Cebriones is Hector’s charioteer, whom Patroclus killed in the previous part. The subject of ἔρυσσαν ‘drew’ is not named: it is the Achaeans, as 780 has just said. ἐκ … ἔρυσσαν and ἀπ’ … ἕλοντο are verbs with their preverbs set apart (tmesis), ‘drew out’ and ‘took off’; τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’. μὲν … δέ sets the Achaeans busy with the body against Patroclus, who goes on. κακὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking evil things’, and ἐνόρουσε is the aorist ‘rushed upon’.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἐπόρουσε θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων, τρὶς δ’ ἐννέα φῶτας ἔπεφνεν.
sentences.l:
Three times then he rushed on, the equal of swift Ares,
terribly crying out, and three times nine men he killed.
sentences.i: Three times he rushed on, the equal of swift Ares, crying out terribly, and three times over he killed nine men.
sentences.n: τρὶς … τρὶς, ‘three times … three times’, sets the rush beside the killing: nine men at each rush, twenty-seven in all, though the Greek says only ‘three times nine’. θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ is ‘the equal of swift Ares’, with the dative after ἀτάλαντος. ἰάχων is the present participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, σμερδαλέα the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘terribly’. ἔπεφνεν is a reduplicated aorist, ‘killed’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος,
ἔνθ’ ἄρα τοι Πάτροκλε φάνη βιότοιο τελευτή·
sentences.l:
But when for the fourth time he rushed on, equal to a divinity,
then indeed to you, Patroclus, appeared the end of life;
sentences.i: But when he rushed on for the fourth time, like a divinity, then, Patroclus, the end of your life showed itself to you;
sentences.n: The poet turns to Patroclus and speaks to him as ‘you’ (τοι is σοι, ‘to you’, not the particle). Line 786 is a line already met: δαίμονι ἶσος is ‘equal to a divinity’, an unnamed power. ἐπέσσυτο is the aorist of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush on’, φάνη the aorist passive of φαίνω ‘appear’, and βιότοιο τελευτή is ‘the end of life’.

sentences.t:
ἤντετο γάρ τοι Φοῖβος ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ
δεινός·
sentences.l:
For met you Phoebus in strong battle,
terrible;
sentences.i: For Phoebus met you in strong battle, terrible;
sentences.n: Phoebus is Apollo, and he is the one who ‘met’ Patroclus: ἤντετο is the imperfect of ἀντάομαι ‘meet’, with τοι = σοι ‘you’ again. κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ is ‘in strong battle’, a stock phrase. δεινός ‘terrible’ begins line 789 by itself, set apart for weight, and the clause ends with it.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν τὸν ἰόντα κατὰ κλόνον οὐκ ἐνόησεν,
ἠέρι γὰρ πολλῇ κεκαλυμμένος ἀντεβόλησε·
sentences.l:
he indeed him coming through the turmoil did not notice,
for in thick mist wrapped he met him;
sentences.i: Patroclus did not notice him coming through the turmoil, for the god, wrapped in thick mist, met him;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν is Patroclus, ‘he for his part’, and τὸν ἰόντα is Apollo ‘coming’, so the subject changes at ἀντεβόλησε, where the god is the one who ‘met’ him. κλόνος is ‘turmoil’, the confusion of the fight. κεκαλυμμένος is the perfect passive participle of καλύπτω ‘cover’, ‘wrapped’, and ἠέρι πολλῇ is a dative of means, ‘in thick mist’ (ἀήρ is the thick air that hides a god).

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ὄπιθεν, πλῆξεν δὲ μετάφρενον εὐρέε τ’ ὤμω
χειρὶ καταπρηνεῖ, στρεφεδίνηθεν δέ οἱ ὄσσε.
sentences.l:
He stood behind, and struck the back and the two broad shoulders
with downturned hand, and were made to spin for him his eyes.
sentences.i: He stood behind him and struck him on the back and the two broad shoulders with the flat of his hand, and his eyes whirled.
sentences.n: The blow that begins Patroclus’ death. στῆ is ἔστη ‘stood’ without the augment. μετάφρενον is the back between the shoulders; ὤμω and εὐρέε are duals, ‘the two broad shoulders’. χειρὶ καταπρηνεῖ is ‘with downturned hand’, a blow with the flat of the hand. στρεφεδίνηθεν is the aorist passive of στρεφεδινέω ‘whirl, spin’, with οἱ ‘for him’ and ὄσσε ‘eyes’ (dual).

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν κρατὸς κυνέην βάλε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: And from his head the helmet cast Phoebus Apollo;
sentences.i: Phoebus Apollo cast the helmet from his head;
sentences.n: ἀπὸ … κρατός is ‘from the head’; ἀπὸ can also be read with βάλε, ‘cast off’ (tmesis). τοῦ … κρατός is the genitive of κάρα ‘head’, ‘his head’, in a form with stem κρατ-. κυνέη is the word for the helmet here (the word is properly a cap of animal skin). Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the god’s whole name and title together.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ κυλινδομένη καναχὴν ἔχε ποσσὶν ὑφ’ ἵππων
αὐλῶπις τρυφάλεια, μιάνθησαν δὲ ἔθειραι
αἵματι καὶ κονίῃσι·
sentences.i: and rolling along, the tubed helmet rang beneath the horses’ feet, and the plumes were defiled with blood and with dust;
sentences.n: ἣ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘it’, the helmet. καναχὴν ἔχε is ‘kept up a ringing’, καναχή being the clang of metal. αὐλῶπις is a word whose meaning is not known for certain: it is built on αὐλός ‘pipe, tube’, and ‘tubed’ follows that root without deciding what the tube was. τρυφάλεια is a word for the helmet, and ἔθειραι are the plumes, the horsehair of the crest. μιάνθησαν is the aorist passive of μιαίνω ‘stain, defile’.

sentences.t:
πάρος γε μὲν οὐ θέμις ἦεν
ἱππόκομον πήληκα μιαίνεσθαι κονίῃσιν,
ἀλλ’ ἀνδρὸς θείοιο κάρη χαρίεν τε μέτωπον
ῥύετ’ Ἀχιλλῆος·
sentences.i: Until then it had not been the custom for the helmet with horsehair plumes to be defiled with dust, but it had guarded the head and lovely forehead of a divine man, Achilles;
sentences.n: πάρος γε μὲν is ‘until now, though’, picking up the helmet’s fall. θέμις is what custom holds right, and οὐ θέμις ἦεν is ‘it was not custom’, with the infinitive μιαίνεσθαι ‘to be defiled’ (the passive of the verb in 795). ἱππόκομον πήληκα is ‘horse-plumed helmet’; πήληξ is another word for the same piece as κυνέη and τρυφάλεια. The helmet is Achilles’ own, which Patroclus wears: ῥύετ’ is the imperfect of ῥύομαι ‘protect’; its object, ‘the head and lovely forehead of a divine man’, stands before it, and the man’s name Ἀχιλλῆος is put after it. The unit ends in the middle of line 799.

sentences.t:
τότε δὲ Ζεὺς Ἕκτορι δῶκεν
ᾗ κεφαλῇ φορέειν, σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ ἦεν ὄλεθρος.
sentences.l:
but then Zeus to Hector gave it
to carry on his own head, and near to him was destruction.
sentences.i: but then Zeus gave it to Hector to wear on his own head, and destruction was close to him.
sentences.n: τότε δέ marks the change: Zeus gave the helmet to Hector φορέειν ‘to carry’ (‘to wear’ in the free English), an infinitive of purpose. ᾗ is the possessive ὅς, ‘his own’, not the relative; κεφαλῇ is the dative ‘on his head’. σχεδόθεν is ‘from close by’, and ἦεν is ἦν ‘was’. The destruction that stands near Hector is his death, which Patroclus foretells at 852.

sentences.t:
πᾶν δέ οἱ ἐν χείρεσσιν ἄγη δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρὸν κεκορυθμένον·
sentences.l:
And all in his hands was shattered the long-shadowed spear,
heavy, great, stout, armed;
sentences.i: In his hands the whole long-shadowed spear was shattered, heavy, great, stout, and armed;
sentences.n: ἄγη is the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’ (the form of ἐάγη), with πᾶν … ἔγχος ‘the whole spear’. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is the stock epithet of the spear, translated the same each time. κεκορυθμένον is the perfect passive participle of κορύσσω ‘arm’, here a spear ‘armed’ with its head. βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρὸν is three bare adjectives in a row, ‘heavy, great, stout’. The unit ends in the middle of line 802.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἀπ’ ὤμων
ἀσπὶς σὺν τελαμῶνι χαμαὶ πέσε τερμιόεσσα.
sentences.l:
and from his shoulders
the shield with its strap fell to the ground, with a border.
sentences.i: and from his shoulders the bordered shield with its shield-strap fell to the ground.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ‘and then’ is epic for δέ. ἀπ’ ὤμων ‘from his shoulders’ goes with πέσε, the unaugmented ἔπεσε ‘fell’. The shield hung by a τελαμών, a strap over the shoulder. τερμιόεσσα is a rare epithet of the shield whose meaning is not known; it is built on τέρμα ‘end, edge’, and ‘with a border’ (‘bordered’) is the guess, as at τερμιόεντα in the Odyssey (19.242).

sentences.t: λῦσε δέ οἱ θώρηκα ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l: And loosed for him his breastplate the lord, the son of Zeus, Apollo.
sentences.i: And lord Apollo, the son of Zeus, unfastened his breastplate.
sentences.n: λῦσε is ‘loosed, undid’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is the dative of the person affected. θώρηκα is the accusative of θώρηξ ‘breastplate’. ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων is a whole-name formula, ‘lord, son of Zeus, Apollo’, translated the same every time.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄτη φρένας εἷλε, λύθεν δ’ ὑπὸ φαίδιμα γυῖα,
στῆ δὲ ταφών·
sentences.l:
And him bewilderment seized in his wits, and were loosed beneath him his glorious limbs,
and he stood, amazed;
sentences.i: Bewilderment seized his wits, his glorious limbs were loosed beneath him, and he stood in amazement;
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ … φρένας are two accusatives, ‘him … in his wits’, the person and the part affected. ἄτη is bewilderment, the clouded mind. λύθεν is the aorist passive ἐλύθησαν, the ending -εν for -ησαν and no augment. φαίδιμα γυῖα are ‘glorious limbs’; φαίδιμος is ‘glorious’ every time. ταφών is the aorist participle of the verb that goes with τάφος ‘amazement’. The unit ends in the middle of line 806.

sentences.t:
ὄπιθεν δὲ μετάφρενον ὀξέϊ δουρὶ
ὤμων μεσσηγὺς σχεδόθεν βάλε Δάρδανος ἀνὴρ
Πανθοΐδης Εὔφορβος, ὃς ἡλικίην ἐκέκαστο
ἔγχεΐ θ’ ἱπποσύνῃ τε πόδεσσί τε καρπαλίμοισι·
sentences.l:
and from behind in the back with sharp spear,
between the shoulders, from close, struck him a Dardanian man,
Panthous’-son Euphorbus, who excelled those of his age
in spear and horsemanship and in quick feet;
sentences.i: and from behind, in the back between the shoulders, a Dardanian man, Euphorbus son of Panthous, struck him from close by with a sharp spear, he who excelled men of his age with the spear, in horsemanship and on his quick feet;
sentences.n: Euphorbus is named only after the verb, last of the three phrases that describe him. ὄπιθεν δὲ μετάφρενον … βάλε is ‘from behind struck in the back’, with ὤμων μεσσηγύς ‘between the shoulders’ (genitive after the preposition-adverb) and σχεδόθεν ‘from close by’. Πανθοΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Panthous’. ὃς ἡλικίην ἐκέκαστο: ἡλικίη is the men of one’s own age, accusative after ἐκέκαστο, a pluperfect used as an imperfect, ‘excelled’. ἔγχεΐ θ’ ἱπποσύνῃ τε πόδεσσί τε are three datives of respect joined by τε, and καρπαλίμοισι is the epic dative plural, ‘quick’.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ δὴ τότε φῶτας ἐείκοσι βῆσεν ἀφ’ ἵππων
πρῶτ’ ἐλθὼν σὺν ὄχεσφι διδασκόμενος πολέμοιο·
sentences.l:
for indeed then twenty men he brought down from their horses
first having come with his chariot, learning war;
sentences.i: for even then, when he first came with his chariot, learning war, he brought twenty men down from their horses;
sentences.n: This explains the praise just given. ἐείκοσι is εἴκοσι ‘twenty’, and βῆσεν is the causative aorist of βαίνω, ‘made go down’, i.e. brought down. ἀφ’ ἵππων ‘from horses’ is taken to mean from their chariots. ὄχεσφι is the dative of ὄχεα with the ending -φι, ‘with a chariot’. διδασκόμενος is the present participle passive of διδάσκω ‘teach’, ‘being taught’, so ‘learning’. πρῶτ’ is πρῶτα ‘first’, elided.

sentences.t:
ὅς τοι πρῶτος ἐφῆκε βέλος Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ
οὐδὲ δάμασσ’·
sentences.l:
He who first at you shot a shaft, Patroclus the horseman,
and did not subdue you;
sentences.i: this was the man who first shot a shaft at you, Patroclus the horseman, and did not overcome you;
sentences.n: ὅς τοι is ‘he who … to you’, again with τοι = σοι. The poet again speaks to Patroclus, and Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ is the vocative of his stock address ‘Patroclus the horseman’, which the poet uses for the second person. ἐφῆκε is the aorist of ἐφίημι ‘shoot at’, and βέλος is ‘shaft’ (the word for a thrown spear or an arrow), here a spear. δάμασσ’ is δάμασσε ‘subdued’, elided. The unit ends in the middle of line 813.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν αὖτις ἀνέδραμε, μίκτο δ’ ὁμίλῳ,
ἐκ χροὸς ἁρπάξας δόρυ μείλινον, οὐδ’ ὑπέμεινε
Πάτροκλον γυμνόν περ ἐόντ’ ἐν δηϊοτῆτι.
sentences.l:
he indeed ran back again, and mingled in the throng,
having snatched from the flesh the ashen spear, and did not await
Patroclus, naked though he was, in the fighting.
sentences.i: he ran back again and mingled with the throng, snatching his ashen spear out of the flesh, and did not wait for Patroclus, naked though he was, in the fighting.
sentences.n: The poet now says ‘Patroclus’ in the third person, having spoken to him in the second three lines before (812). ἀνέδραμε is the aorist of ἀνατρέχω ‘run back up’, and μίκτο is ἐμίκτο ‘mingled’, without the augment. ἐκ χροὸς is ‘out of the flesh’, ἁρπάξας ‘having snatched’, and μείλινον is ‘ashen’, of ash-wood. γυμνόν is ‘naked’, i.e. stripped of armour by Apollo; the whole phrase γυμνόν περ ἐόντ’ is ‘though he was naked’, with περ and ἐόντα (ἐών) for ὤν. δηϊοτής is ‘fighting’.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δὲ θεοῦ πληγῇ καὶ δουρὶ δαμασθεὶς
ἂψ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο κῆρ’ ἀλεείνων.
sentences.l:
And Patroclus, by the god’s blow and by the spear subdued,
back to the company of his companions he drew away, death-fate avoiding.
sentences.i: Patroclus, overcome by the god’s blow and by the spear, drew back into the company of his companions, shunning death.
sentences.n: θεοῦ πληγῇ ‘the god’s blow’ and δουρί are two datives of means with the participle δαμασθείς ‘subdued’ (aorist passive). Line 817 is Iliad 3.32 without the δ’, and keeps that line’s English: ἐχάζετο is the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘give ground’, here ‘drew away’. ἔθνος ἑτάρων is ‘the company of companions’, ἑτάρων being ἑταίρων. κῆρ’ is κῆρα ‘death-fate’, the accusative of κήρ, the doom that comes with death, the object of ἀλεείνων ‘shunning’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς εἶδεν Πατροκλῆα μεγάθυμον
ἂψ ἀναχαζόμενον βεβλημένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
ἀγχίμολόν ῥά οἱ ἦλθε κατὰ στίχας, οὖτα δὲ δουρὶ
νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα, διὰ πρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσε·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when he saw Patroclus great-hearted
back, drawing back, struck with the sharp bronze,
close by him came through the ranks, and wounded him with his spear
to the lowest flank, and straight through drove the bronze;
sentences.i: When Hector saw great-hearted Patroclus drawing back, struck by the sharp bronze, he came close by him through the ranks and stabbed him with his spear into the lowest part of the flank, and drove the bronze straight through;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς εἶδεν is ‘and when Hector saw’, with Πατροκλῆα, the Ionic accusative, and the stock epithet μεγάθυμον ‘great-hearted’. Two participles follow, ἀναχαζόμενον ‘drawing back’ and βεβλημένον ‘struck’ (perfect passive of βάλλω). ἀγχίμολον … οἱ ἦλθε is ‘came close by him’. οὖτα is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’ (it has no augment), νείατον ἐς κενεῶνα ‘into the lowest flank’, the soft part below the ribs. διὰ πρὸ is a doubled preverb, ‘right through’, with ἔλασσε ‘drove’; χαλκόν ‘bronze’ stands for the spear-point.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, μέγα δ’ ἤκαχε λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud, and greatly grieved the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: He fell with a thud, and brought great grief on the army of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: δούπησεν is ‘fell with a thud’, from δοῦπος ‘thud’, with πεσών ‘falling’. ἤκαχε is the aorist of ἀκαχίζω ‘grieve’, with μέγα as the adverb ‘greatly’. λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the people (the army) of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε σῦν ἀκάμαντα λέων ἐβιήσατο χάρμῃ,
ὥ τ’ ὄρεος κορυφῇσι μέγα φρονέοντε μάχεσθον
πίδακος ἀμφ’ ὀλίγης·
sentences.i: As when a lion overpowers a tireless boar in the joy of battle, the two of them, full of proud thoughts, fighting on a mountain’s peaks over a little spring;
sentences.n: The simile compares Hector to the lion and Patroclus to the boar. ὡς δ’ ὅτε is the epic opening ‘and as when’. ἐβιήσατο is an aorist used for what is always so, so English has the present ‘overpowers’; σῦν is the accusative of σῦς ‘boar’, ἀκάμαντα ‘tireless’, and χάρμῃ ‘in the joy of battle’. ὥ τ’ is the dual of the relative with τε, ‘who, the two’. The next words have a dual verb, μάχεσθον ‘fight’, as in the lion simile at 756–758. ὄρεος is the genitive of ὄρος ‘mountain’, κορυφῇσι the dative plural ‘on the peaks’, and πίδακος ἀμφ’ ὀλίγης ‘about a little spring’.

sentences.t: ἐθέλουσι δὲ πιέμεν ἄμφω·
sentences.l: and both wish to drink;
sentences.i: both of them wish to drink;
sentences.n: ἐθέλουσι is the third plural of ἐθέλω ‘wish’ without a contraction. πιέμεν is the aorist infinitive of πίνω ‘drink’ in the epic ending -μεν (Attic πιεῖν), and ἄμφω is ‘both’ (nominative, dual in sense).

sentences.t: πολλὰ δέ τ’ ἀσθμαίνοντα λέων ἐδάμασσε βίηφιν·
sentences.l: and him panting much the lion subdued by his might;
sentences.i: and the lion overcomes him as he pants hard, by sheer might;
sentences.n: The aorist ἐδάμασσε is again for what always happens, ‘overcomes’ in plain English. ἀσθμαίνοντα is the accusative participle ‘panting’, the boar. πολλά is the adverb ‘much, hard’, and βίηφιν is βίη with the ending -φιν, ‘by might’. δέ τ’ is the connective with the particle used in general statements.

sentences.t:
ὣς πολέας πεφνόντα Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱὸν
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης σχεδὸν ἔγχεϊ θυμὸν ἀπηύρα,
καί οἱ ἐπευχόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So him who had killed many, Menoetius’ sturdy son,
Hector Priam’s-son from close by with his spear took away his life,
and over him, vaunting, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So, with his spear at close quarters, Hector, son of Priam, took the life of Menoetius’ sturdy son, who had killed so many, and in triumph spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ὣς answers ὡς δ’ ὅτε of 823: the simile is closed. πολέας is πολλούς ‘many’, and πεφνόντα is the aorist participle of φένω ‘kill’ (the reduplicated ἔπεφνον); it agrees with υἱόν, ‘him who had killed many’. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱόν is the stock phrase ‘Menoetius’ sturdy son’, Patroclus. ἀπηύρα is the imperfect of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, with θυμὸν ‘his life’. ἐπευχόμενος is ‘vaunting’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘spoke winged words’ is the formula that introduces a speech.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλ’ ἦ που ἔφησθα πόλιν κεραϊξέμεν ἁμήν,
Τρωϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ἀπούρας
ἄξειν ἐν νήεσσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
νήπιε·
sentences.l:
“Patroclus, surely you said that our city you would ravage,
and the Trojan women, the day of freedom having taken away,
to carry in ships to your dear fatherland,
foolish one;
sentences.i: “Patroclus, surely you said that you would ravage our city, take from the Trojan women the day of freedom, and carry them in ships to your dear fatherland, foolish one;
sentences.n: Hector begins his taunt. Πάτροκλ’ is the vocative, elided. ἦ που ἔφησθα is ‘surely you said’, with the old second-person ending -σθα, and what follows is reported in the infinitive: κεραϊξέμεν (the future infinitive of κεραΐζω ‘ravage, lay waste’), ἄξειν ‘would carry off’. ἁμήν is an epic form of ‘our’. ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ἀπούρας is ‘having taken away the day of freedom’; ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to the dear fatherland’, his own, hence ‘your’ in English, νήεσσι the epic dative plural of ναῦς ‘ships’. νήπιε is ‘foolish one’, said to a man who has acted blindly. The unit ends in the middle of line 833.

sentences.t:
τάων δὲ πρόσθ’ Ἕκτορος ὠκέες ἵπποι
ποσσὶν ὀρωρέχαται πολεμίζειν·
sentences.l:
but in front of them Hector’s swift horses
with their feet are stretched out to fight;
sentences.i: but in front of them Hector’s swift horses are straining forward on their feet for the fight;
sentences.n: τάων is the feminine genitive plural ‘of those’, i.e. the women, after πρόσθ’ ‘in front of’. ὠκέες ἵπποι is ‘swift horses’. ὀρωρέχαται is the perfect middle of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’, ‘are stretched out, are straining’, with πολεμίζειν ‘to fight’ as its purpose and ποσσίν the epic dative plural of πούς ‘foot’. The unit ends in the middle of line 834.

sentences.t:
ἔγχεϊ δ’ αὐτὸς
Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισι μεταπρέπω, ὅ σφιν ἀμύνω
ἦμαρ ἀναγκαῖον·
sentences.i: and I myself am conspicuous with the spear among the war-loving Trojans, in that I ward off from them the day of necessity;
sentences.n: αὐτός is ‘I myself’. μεταπρέπω is ‘am conspicuous among’, with the dative Τρωσὶ φιλοπτολέμοισι ‘the war-loving Trojans’. ὅ is the neuter of the relative used as a conjunction, ‘in that’. σφιν is the epic dative of the pronoun, ‘for them’, and ἀμύνω ‘ward off’ takes the accusative ἦμαρ. ἦμαρ ἀναγκαῖον, ‘the day of necessity’, is the counterpart of the ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ of 831: the day that is forced on a man, which the Trojans are spared. The unit ends in the middle of line 836.

sentences.t: σὲ δέ τ’ ἐνθάδε γῦπες ἔδονται.
sentences.l: but you here the vultures will eat.
sentences.i: but you the vultures will eat here.
sentences.n: ἔδονται is the future of ἔδω ‘eat’ in the middle form, ‘will eat’. σὲ is put first and strongly for contrast with the Trojans just spoken of, and ἐνθάδε is ‘here’. τε is a connecting particle.

sentences.t:
ἆ δείλ’, οὐδέ τοι ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν χραίσμησεν Ἀχιλλεύς,
ὅς πού τοι μάλα πολλὰ μένων ἐπετέλλετ’ ἰόντι·
sentences.l:
Oh, miserable one, not even Achilles, good though he is, helped you,
he who surely, remaining behind, laid many charges on you as you went:
sentences.i: Oh, miserable man, Achilles, good as he is, was no help to you, he who, I think, gave you many charges as you went, while he stayed behind:
sentences.n: ἆ δείλ’ is the cry of address, ‘oh, miserable one’, with δειλός ‘miserable’. χραίσμησεν is the aorist of χραισμέω ‘help, avail’, and ἐσθλὸς ἐών is ‘good though he is’. πού is ‘I think, surely’. μένων is ‘remaining behind’, at the ships, and ἐπετέλλετ’ is the imperfect middle of ἐπιτέλλομαι ‘lay a charge on’, with ἰόντι ‘as you went’ in the dative, agreeing with τοι (= σοι). The speech Hector quotes comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
μή μοι πρὶν ἰέναι Πατρόκλεες ἱπποκέλευθε
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυρὰς πρὶν Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
αἱματόεντα χιτῶνα περὶ στήθεσσι δαΐξαι.
sentences.l:
‘Do not to me go sooner, Patroclus, horse-urging one,
to the hollow ships, than that of man-slaying Hector
the blood-stained tunic about his chest you have torn.’
sentences.i: ‘Do not come to me, to the hollow ships, Patroclus, you who urge horses on, until you have torn the blood-stained tunic about the chest of man-slaying Hector.’
sentences.n: Hector quotes Achilles’ charge inside his own speech, so the English shows it in single quotation marks. μή with the infinitive ἰέναι ‘go’ is a command, and πρὶν … πρίν, ‘sooner … than’, give the condition: not before you have torn (δαΐξαι, aorist infinitive of δαΐζω ‘tear’). ἱπποκέλευθε is the vocative ‘horse-urging one’, a stock epithet of Patroclus; ἀνδροφόνοιο is ‘man-slaying’; νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is ‘to the hollow ships’, ἔπι placed after its noun. αἱματόεντα is ‘blood-stained’, the epic -όεις adjective.

sentences.t: ὥς πού σε προσέφη, σοὶ δὲ φρένας ἄφρονι πεῖθε.
sentences.l: So surely he addressed you, and you in your wits, senseless one, he persuaded.”
sentences.i: So, I suppose, he spoke to you, and persuaded your wits, senseless as you are.”
sentences.n: ὥς πού σε προσέφη is ‘so, I suppose, he spoke to you’; πού is the same particle as in 838. σοὶ … ἄφρονι is ‘you, senseless’ in the dative, with φρένας ‘your wits’ as the accusative of the part affected, and πεῖθε the imperfect of πείθω ‘persuade’. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὀλιγοδρανέων προσέφης Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ·
sentences.l: Him, weak, you addressed, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.i: Weak as he was, you said to him, Patroclus the horseman:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the poet again addresses Patroclus as ‘you’: προσέφης is the second-person aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’, and Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ the stock vocative. ὀλιγοδρανέων, ‘weak’, is the participle of a verb built on ὀλίγος ‘little’, ‘with little strength’.

sentences.t: ἤδη νῦν Ἕκτορ μεγάλ’ εὔχεο·
sentences.l: “Now already, Hector, boast greatly;
sentences.i: “Even now, Hector, boast greatly;
sentences.n: Patroclus’ last speech begins. ἤδη νῦν is ‘even now’, with a bitter edge. εὔχεο is the imperative of εὔχομαι ‘boast’, with the uncontracted ending -εο, and μεγάλ’ is the neuter plural μεγάλα used as an adverb, ‘greatly’. The unit ends in the middle of line 844.

sentences.t:
σοὶ γὰρ ἔδωκε
νίκην Ζεὺς Κρονίδης καὶ Ἀπόλλων, οἵ με δάμασσαν
ῥηιδίως·
sentences.i: for Zeus, the son of Cronus, and Apollo gave you the victory, they who overcame me easily;
sentences.n: The verb ἔδωκε ‘gave’ is singular though it has two subjects, Ζεὺς Κρονίδης and Ἀπόλλων, agreeing with the nearer; Κρονίδης is ‘son of Cronus’. νίκην is ‘victory’. οἵ με δάμασσαν is ‘who subdued me’, δάμασσαν being ἐδάμασσαν without the augment, and ῥηιδίως ‘easily’ is Attic ῥᾳδίως. The unit ends in the middle of line 846.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ γὰρ ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἕλοντο.
sentences.l: for they themselves from my shoulders took the armour.
sentences.i: for they themselves took the armour from my shoulders.
sentences.n: αὐτοί is ‘they themselves’, the two gods. The words ἀπ’ ὤμων τεύχε’ ἕλοντο are those of 782, said there of Cebriones: the armour is stripped from a dead man’s shoulders there, from a dying man’s here.

sentences.t:
τοιοῦτοι δ’ εἴ πέρ μοι ἐείκοσιν ἀντεβόλησαν,
πάντές κ’ αὐτόθ’ ὄλοντο ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ δαμέντες.
sentences.l:
But even if twenty such as these had met me,
all of them would have perished there, subdued under my spear.
sentences.i: Even if twenty such men as these had met me, all of them would have died right there, overcome by my spear.
sentences.n: τοιοῦτοι ‘such as these’ points to men of the sort who have just struck him down; the claim is that mortals alone could not have done it. εἴ πέρ … ἀντεβόλησαν is a condition in the past with an aorist, and κ’ … ὄλοντο, κε with the aorist, gives the result, ‘would have perished’. ἐείκοσιν is εἴκοσι, and αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι ‘right there’, elided. δαμέντες is the aorist passive participle ‘subdued’, and ἐμῷ is the possessive ‘my’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καὶ Λητοῦς ἔκτανεν υἱός,
ἀνδρῶν δ’ Εὔφορβος·
sentences.l:
But me baneful fate and Leto’s son killed,
and of men Euphorbus;
sentences.i: But it was baneful fate and the son of Leto who killed me, and among men Euphorbus;
sentences.n: Three killers are named in turn: μοῖρ’ ὀλοή ‘baneful fate’ (μοῖρα, the elided form here), Λητοῦς υἱός ‘Leto’s son’, i.e. Apollo, left unnamed, and ἀνδρῶν … Εὔφορβος ‘Euphorbus among men’ (ἀνδρῶν is partitive). ἔκτανεν is ‘killed’, a singular verb with the nearest subject. The unit ends in the middle of line 850.

sentences.t: σὺ δέ με τρίτος ἐξεναρίζεις.
sentences.l: and you third are despoiling me.
sentences.i: and you, third, are stripping me of my armour.
sentences.n: σὺ δέ is ‘and you’, in contrast to the three just named, and τρίτος ‘as the third’. ἐξεναρίζεις is the present of ἐξεναρίζω, which is ‘kill and strip of armour’; the killing already being told, the literal line says only ‘despoil’ and the English ‘strip of armour’.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and ἐρέω is the future of λέγω ‘I will say’. βάλλεο is the uncontracted imperative of βάλλομαι ‘lay down (in one’s mind)’, ἐνὶ φρεσὶ … σῇσιν ‘in your own mind’ with σῇσιν the epic dative plural of σός, ‘your own’. The line is already met elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
οὔ θην οὐδ’ αὐτὸς δηρὸν βέῃ, ἀλλά τοι ἤδη
ἄγχι παρέστηκεν θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιὴ
χερσὶ δαμέντ’ Ἀχιλῆος ἀμύμονος Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.l:
Surely not even you yourself will live long, but to you already
near has taken its stand death and strong fate,
you to be subdued by the hands of Achilles, blameless descendant of Aeacus.”
sentences.i: You yourself will not live long either; already death and strong fate stand close beside you, and you will be overcome by the hands of Achilles, blameless descendant of Aeacus.”
sentences.n: The prophecy of Hector’s death. οὔ θην is ‘surely not’, οὐδ’ αὐτός ‘not even you yourself’. βέῃ is a rare epic form of the verb of ‘living’ (βίος), and has the force of a future, ‘you will live’. παρέστηκεν is the perfect of παρίστημι, ‘has taken its stand beside’, i.e. is at hand, with a singular verb for two subjects, θάνατος and μοῖρα κραταιή ‘strong fate’. χερσὶ δαμέντ’ is the accusative participle ‘subdued by the hands’, agreeing with a ‘you’ left out. Ἀχιλῆος ἀμύμονος Αἰακίδαο: ἀμύμων is ‘blameless’, a stock epithet whose sense is not known, and Αἰακίδαο is the epic genitive of Αἰακίδης ‘descendant of Aeacus’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα μιν εἰπόντα τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψε·
sentences.l: So then, as he spoke, the end of death covered him;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the end that death brings covered him;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἄρα μιν εἰπόντα is ‘so then, as he said this’, with μιν ‘him’ in the accusative and the aorist participle of εἶπον. τέλος θανάτοιο κάλυψε is ‘the end of death covered’, said of the end that death brings, with κάλυψε the aorist of καλύπτω ‘cover’.

sentences.t:
ψυχὴ δ’ ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη Ἄϊδος δὲ βεβήκει
ὃν πότμον γοόωσα λιποῦσ’ ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην.
sentences.l:
and the soul out of his limbs, having flown, to Hades went,
bewailing its doom, leaving manhood and youth.
sentences.i: and his soul flew from his limbs and went to the house of Hades, wailing its doom, leaving manhood and youth.
sentences.n: The soul leaves the body: ψυχή is what survives, ῥεθέων ‘limbs’ (a poetic word for the body’s parts) the body it leaves. πταμένη is the aorist participle of πέτομαι ‘fly’. Ἄϊδος δὲ is the genitive Ἄϊδος with the ending -δε of motion toward, ‘to (the house of) Hades’, and βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, used as ‘went’. ὃν πότμον is ‘its own doom’ (ὅς is possessive), γοόωσα is the participle of γοάω ‘wail over’. ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην is ‘manhood and youth’. Line 857 is metrically irregular as transmitted: ἀνδροτῆτα has a syllable closed by a consonant that has to be scanned short, and καὶ is shortened before the vowel of ἥβην.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ τεθνηῶτα προσηύδα φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: To him even dead spoke glorious Hector:
sentences.i: Glorious Hector spoke to him even though he was dead:
sentences.n: τὸν καὶ τεθνηῶτα is ‘him, even dead’; τεθνηῶτα is the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, ‘having died’. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, and φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: Πατρόκλεις τί νύ μοι μαντεύεαι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον;
sentences.l: “Patroclus, why now to me do you prophesy steep destruction?
sentences.i: “Patroclus, why are you prophesying steep destruction for me?
sentences.n: Hector’s answer is a question. Πατρόκλεις is the vocative, an alternative form of Πατρόκλεες used in 812 and 839. μαντεύεαι is the present of μαντεύομαι ‘prophesy’, with the uncontracted ending -εαι. αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον is ‘steep destruction’, the stock phrase; αἰπύς is ‘steep, sheer’.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κ’ Ἀχιλεὺς Θέτιδος πάϊς ἠϋκόμοιο
φθήῃ ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ τυπεὶς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσαι;
sentences.l:
And who knows if Achilles, the child of fine-haired Thetis,
may be first to lose his life, struck beneath my spear?”
sentences.i: Who knows whether Achilles, the child of fine-haired Thetis, may be the first to lose his life, struck beneath my spear?”
sentences.n: τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κ’ is ‘who knows if perhaps’, with κ’ for κε and an elided οἶδε. φθήῃ is the subjunctive of φθάνω ‘be first’, with an infinitive, ὀλέσσαι ‘to lose’ (ἀπὸ … ὀλέσσαι is ‘lose utterly’, the preverb set apart); ‘life’ is θυμόν. τυπεὶς is the aorist passive participle of τύπτω ‘strike’. Θέτιδος πάϊς is ‘child of Thetis’, with ἠϋκόμοιο the epic genitive ‘fine-haired’ (ἠΰκομος), and the diaeresis is kept as printed. Hector’s second speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας δόρυ χάλκεον ἐξ ὠτειλῆς
εἴρυσε λὰξ προσβάς, τὸν δ’ ὕπτιον ὦσ’ ἀπὸ δουρός.
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, the bronze spear out of the wound
he drew, stepping on him with his heel, and him on his back he thrust off the spear.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and setting his heel on him, he drew the bronze spear out of the wound and thrust him off the spear on to his back.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is the formula that closes a speech, ‘so then, having spoken’. ὠτειλῆς is the genitive of ὠτειλή ‘wound’. εἴρυσε is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw’, λὰξ προσβάς ‘setting his heel on’ (the aorist participle of προσβαίνω), and ὦσ’ is ὦσε, the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’. ὕπτιον is ‘on his back’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δὲ ξὺν δουρὶ μετ’ Αὐτομέδοντα βεβήκει
ἀντίθεον θεράποντα ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο·
sentences.l:
And at once with his spear after Automedon he went,
the godlike attendant of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.i: At once, spear in hand, he went after Automedon, the godlike attendant of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.n: Hector goes after Achilles’ charioteer. ξὺν is the epic form of σὺν, and μετ’ … βεβήκει, ‘went after’ (a pluperfect used as an aorist). ἀντίθεον θεράποντα is ‘godlike attendant’, and ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο ‘the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus’ is Achilles, named by his stock epithet.

sentences.t: ἵετο γὰρ βαλέειν·
sentences.l: for he was eager to strike;
sentences.i: for he longed to strike him;
sentences.n: ἵετο is the imperfect middle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, with the infinitive βαλέειν ‘to strike’ (Attic βαλεῖν). Hector is the subject. The reader fills in ‘him’, Automedon.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἔκφερον ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἄμβροτοι, οὓς Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα.
sentences.l:
but him the swift horses bore out,
deathless, which to Peleus the gods gave, splendid gifts.
sentences.i: but the swift, deathless horses, which the gods gave to Peleus as splendid gifts, were carrying Automedon out.
sentences.n: τὸν is Automedon, the object of ἔκφερον ‘were carrying out’. Line 866 stands elsewhere in the poem, where the horses carry Hector off; here the English names Automedon. ἄμβροτοι is ‘deathless’, and the relative οὓς has ἵπποι as its antecedent. δόσαν is ἔδοσαν ‘gave’ without the augment, Πηλῆϊ the dative of Πηλεύς, and ἀγλαὰ δῶρα ‘splendid gifts’ is in apposition to the horses.
